analysis.one_liner: Delayed the 2005 bankruptcy law by two years so Hurricane Katrina survivors could file under older, more forgiving rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House subcommittees and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: In September 2005, just weeks after Hurricane Katrina, Rep. Louise Slaughter proposed pushing back the start date of the new 2005 bankruptcy law by two years. That law, which took effect in October 2005, made it harder for people to wipe out debts in bankruptcy. The delay — retroactive to September 1, 2005 — would have let Gulf Coast families buried in disaster debts file under the older, easier rules instead of the new ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Hurricane Katrina survivors and other Gulf Coast households facing unpayable debts after the storm. The 2005 bankruptcy law imposed a 'means test' and extra paperwork that pushed many filers into a harder repayment track. By keeping the pre-2005 bankruptcy rules available for two more years, the bill would have let disaster victims discharge their debts under the older, more forgiving process.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gulf Coast families with disaster debts

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the 2005 bankruptcy law (BAPCPA) to move its general effective date from 180 days to 910 days after enactment, keeping the older bankruptcy law available for two more years. [S2] [S3]
It takes effect retroactively as of September 1, 2005, making victims of Hurricane Katrina eligible to file under the pre-2005 bankruptcy law. [S2]

The older law had no means test that steers filers toward a repayment plan, so people whose income was wiped out by the disaster could more easily erase medical bills, credit card debts, and other obligations. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers and other consumer lenders. The 2005 law was the credit industry's top legislative priority, and delaying it two years would have meant more debts discharged under the older rules rather than repaid — particularly debts owed by Gulf Coast borrowers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders

drawbacks.text: The delay was not limited to disaster victims: amending the general effective date meant every bankruptcy filer nationwide, not just Katrina survivors, could use the older law for two more years. [S3]
Supporters of the 2005 law argued its means test prevents people with the ability to repay from simply walking away from debts; a two-year blanket delay postponed those safeguards for everyone. [S3]
Even under the older law, filing bankruptcy has lasting consequences for credit and assets; the bill offered debt relief but no other recovery aid such as housing or grants. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Gulf Coast families, the benefit was substantial and urgent: the new bankruptcy law's means test and higher filing costs landed exactly when tens of thousands of households had lost jobs, homes, and income through no fault of their own. The main cost fell on lenders, who would have collected less from disaster victims for two years, and the main design flaw is that the relief was nationwide rather than targeted to the disaster zone. On balance, a well-aimed but broad temporary fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Louise Slaughter introduced the bill on September 6, 2005, less than two weeks after Hurricane Katrina struck the Gulf Coast. [S1] [S5]
It was referred to both the Judiciary Committee and the Financial Services Committee, splitting jurisdiction over its provisions. [S5]
On September 19, 2005, it was sent to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law and the Financial Services Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit. [S5]
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2007. [S1] [S5]
The 2005 bankruptcy law it sought to delay took effect on schedule in October 2005, so Gulf Coast debtors had to file under the new, stricter rules. [S2] [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers and other consumer lenders, who got to apply the stricter 2005 bankruptcy law to Gulf Coast debtors on the original schedule. Disaster victims gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders

for.name: Louise Slaughter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 6, 2005, days after the new bankruptcy law's effective date loomed over Katrina survivors.

for.name: 18 of 435 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat.

against.name: House Judiciary and Financial Services Committees
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees on September 19, 2005, and never reported it out or scheduled any hearing or vote.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House schedule in the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Allowed the new bankruptcy law to take effect on schedule and never brought the delay bill to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: The 2005 bankruptcy law was the credit industry's chief legislative win that year, raising the cost and difficulty of discharging debts. This bill would have suspended its effects for two years, letting disaster-struck borrowers erase more debts — a direct loss of collections for lenders. The bill died, so the new law applied to Gulf Coast debtors as scheduled. [S2] [S3]
